The package `vgi4bio` contains functions for the combined analysis of opportunistic and standardized dataset to estimate relative abundances of multiple species, and habitat preferences.  
  


# The Aquitaine data set

The Aquitaine dataset is used to illustrate several methods. It is stored as a data.frame and contains the data used to develop the models in @Giraud2015 and @Coron2018. 

```{r, eval=F}
library(vgi4bio)
data(Aquitaine)
```

The data.frame Aquitaine contains the following variables (for a complete list of variables, see the suggested citation):

*Species*: this variable stores the code of the bird species. This code is formed by concatenating the first three letters of the genus and the first three letters of the species (see the first column of Table 1 in the main text);  

*Site*: this variable stores the code of the 63 ACT sites used for the model fit;  

*Species\_in\_ACT*: 1 if the species is monitored by the ACT programme, 0 otherwise (for these species, *X\_ACT* is a structural zero, not an absence);

*Effort\_ACT*: the number of listening points-years implemented in the ACT program for the site stored in the variable *Site*;  

*X\_ACT*: the abundance of the species stored in the variable *Species* detected in the site stored in the
  variable *Site* by the ACT program;  

*X\_LPO*: the abundance of the species stored in the variable *Species* detected in the site stored in the variable *Site* by the opportunistic LPO program;


# Fit the combination model

In this example, we consider the model combining the 'complete' ACT dataset (standardized data, known sampling effort) and the LPO dataset (opportunistic data, unknown sampling effort), as in @Giraud2015. For other combinations of data, see @Giraud2015.

First, we format the data for the fit. Only the species monitored by ACT (`Species_in_ACT == 1`) contribute ACT counts: for the other species, the zeros in `X_ACT` mean "not recorded", not "absent", and must be left out.

```{r, eval=F}
inACT <- Aquitaine$Species_in_ACT == 1
df <- rbind(
  data.frame(species = Aquitaine$Species[inACT], site = Aquitaine$Site[inACT],
             N_obs = Aquitaine$X_ACT[inACT], effort = Aquitaine$Effort_ACT[inACT],
             dataset = "ACT"),
  data.frame(species = Aquitaine$Species, site = Aquitaine$Site,
             N_obs = Aquitaine$X_LPO, effort = 1, dataset = "LPO"))
```

The function `fun_abund_estim()` fits the model. The argument `standardized` gives the dataset whose sampling effort is known: its site effects are fixed by the `effort` offset, while the site effects of the opportunistic dataset are estimated. Fitting the model on the full data set takes a few minutes (one parameter per species x site combination).

```{r, eval=F}
abund.mod <- fun_abund_estim(df = df, standardized = "ACT", family = "quasipoisson")
# model summary
summary(abund.mod$mod)
```

# Extract the relative abundances

The function `fun_rel_abund()` extracts the relative abundance of each species on each site, with confidence intervals. Abundances are only identifiable up to a species-specific constant: by default (`scale = "sum"`), they are rescaled to sum to one across sites for each species. This is available for all species, including the 21 species recorded only by the LPO.

```{r, eval=F}
ra <- fun_rel_abund(abund.mod)
head(ra)
# the 5 sites with the highest relative abundance of the blackbird
tm <- ra[ra$species == "TURMER", ]
head(tm[order(-tm$rel_abund), ], 5)
```

With `scale = "none"`, the abundances are expressed as expected counts per unit of effort of the standardized dataset (here, per ACT point-count-year). This scale is only defined for the species monitored by ACT.

```{r, eval=F}
ra_act <- fun_rel_abund(abund.mod, scale = "none")
```

# Assess the model against an independent reference

The STOC programme surveyed 24 of the 63 sites and was not used for the fit: it provides an independent reference. We use `fun_pearsons()` and `fun_braycurt()` to compare, species by species, the estimated relative abundances with the STOC abundances (*N_ref*), on these 24 sites.

```{r, eval=F}
ref <- Aquitaine[Aquitaine$Site_in_STOC == 1, ]
ref$N_ref <- ref$X_STOC / ref$Effort_STOC
m <- merge(ra, ref[, c("Species", "Site", "N_ref")],
           by.x = c("species", "site"), by.y = c("Species", "Site"))

# species monitored by ACT
act <- m[m$in_standardized, ]
fun_pearsons(N_pred = act$rel_abund, N_ref = act$N_ref, newdata = act)
fun_braycurt(N_pred = act$rel_abund, N_ref = act$N_ref, newdata = act)

# species recorded only by LPO
lpo <- m[!m$in_standardized, ]
fun_pearsons(N_pred = lpo$rel_abund, N_ref = lpo$N_ref, newdata = lpo)
fun_braycurt(N_pred = lpo$rel_abund, N_ref = lpo$N_ref, newdata = lpo)
```

The median (first and third quartiles) Pearson correlation is 0.55 (0.38–0.68) for the 13 species monitored by ACT and 0.35 (0.19–0.47) for the 21 other species, as reported in Table 2 of @Giraud2015.

Replacing the complete ACT data by the reduced dataset `X_ACTred` (one point-count-year per site, so `effort = 1`) gives 0.54 (0.25–0.61) and 0.28 (0.08–0.40), also as in @Giraud2015.
